input:
I developed this practical map from the rest of the method. Treat the complete sequence as a provisional synthesis: some components have direct research behind them, while the full arrangement is my own:

1. The child alone: orient to the present and establish enough outside safety to begin.
2. The child with a borrowed adult: experience one reliable adult function through a real, remembered, imagined, or symbolic figure.
3. The adult apprentice: care for the child together with support and do at least one part yourself.
4. The inner adult: repeat warmth, protection, and direction until those capacities become familiar enough to summon.
5. The adult and child in relationship: the adult leads without exiling the child, and the child no longer has to run the whole life alone.

You don’t have to stop being the child. You become larger than the child-state. A useful sentence is: “I am still this child, and I am also becoming the adult who stays.”

emulate.text:
NB I’ve developed this map more practically in the rest of the method, which is why I’m comfortable publishing this provisional synthesis (parts of which are directly research based, the whole of which is my own):

i) child on her own – orientation and external safety

ii) child with borrowed adult – experience of at least one good adult function, personified by a real/remembered/imagined/symbolic figure

iii) adult as apprentice – with help, adult tries to do at least one part of looking after the child

iv) adult in her own right – adult repeats as many times as necessary, to build up the capacity to summon it at will: offering the child warmth, protection and direction

v) adult in relation to child – adult in charge but not banishing child, child no longer solely responsible for managing life

The child doesn’t need to stop being a child – you just become bigger than the child-state. A useful saying to yourself might be: ‘I don’t need to stop being this child, but I am also becoming an adult…’

input:
You might notice the hook before you have any clue what part of you is doing the hooking. Or you might notice it embarrassingly late. The jaw is already tight, the stomach is already involved, half the text is written—and then you remember you're supposed to be observing yourself. Maybe forget the detective work for a minute. Child, protector, old wound... you can figure that out later. Sometimes the hand is already going toward a drink, or you've vanished into scrolling, or you're halfway through deciding what the entire relationship means. Pema Chödrön calls this tightening and urge before the story has finished forming *shenpa*.

When you catch it, look around and say you're hooked. If nobody is in danger, take a breath or three before you finish the thing you were doing. You do not need those breaths to settle the case. Maybe there's enough adult around to be nice to the kid for a second. Or enough Protector to stop something stupid. Or maybe all you've got is “not yet,” which is still more useful than sending the message from inside the reaction.

Sometimes it may be a bit later, perhaps after we’ve noticed the tightening in our jaw or the getting involved of our stomach and the writing of half of the text message we really, really shouldn’t be sending. In which case it may be a good idea to forget about finding out who’s hooked for the moment – Child, Protector, past hurt. Our hand may already be reaching for a glass of wine or turning to our phones or forming an opinion about our relationship. Pema Chodron has a great word for this tightening/urge – shenpa.

So, let’s just notice that we’ve been hooked. If we can take a breath or two (or three) and finish what we were doing (assuming no-one is in danger) all the better. If we don’t manage to take the breaths to settle down, we may at least have time to summon enough Adult to be nice to the Child, or Protector to stop us doing something stupid, or simply say to ourselves ‘not yet’.

You might barely have spontaneous words in your mind and still be perfectly capable of thinking a sentence on purpose. Try it and see. If words are there, use them; say the thing aloud, write it, whatever gets it out of the strange imaginary-conversation zone. And if that starts feeling like homework you're doing for a child who isn't answering, drop it. Maybe what's actually happening is a knot in your stomach, an urge to leave, some image that keeps coming up, a song that suddenly feels relevant. Sometimes nothing “answers” and you just know what would be kind.

The order gets murky too. Feeling can precede language, language can expose a feeling, and afterward you may not know which happened first. I don't think you need to solve that before using whatever words eventually help you understand it.

input:
Sexual exclusivity got much more important once agriculture, property and inheritance entered the picture. By the Industrial Revolution, the strict version was everywhere, with law and social pressure behind it. Plenty of tribal cultures have been much looser about what could happen outside a primary partnership, including other sexual or emotional relationships. There’s a term for some of that: social monogamy.

I took exclusivity further than that. B. wanted to marry me, but I was still attracted to other women, and somehow I decided that meant I shouldn’t marry her yet. I told her, “It’s not fair of me to commit to you if I’m still attracted to other women, so before I do, let me see if I can fix that.”

emulate.text:
Monogamy, particularly the sexual aspect of it, has become much more important since agriculture, and the advent of property and inheritance. By the Industrial Revolution it was being universally enforced in some strict form, often through both law and social pressure. Prior to that, there were many tribal cultures that were far more relaxed about allowing sexual and even emotional contact with others outside of the primary partnership. I believe the term "social monogamy" has been coined to describe this.

I took this idea to its logical extreme. I told B, when she told me she wanted to marry me, that although I wanted to marry her, I was still sexually attracted to other women. Thus I felt that it would not be right for me to marry her until I could fix that. My actual words to her were, "It's not fair of me to commit to you while I am still sexually attracted to other women, so it's necessary for me to work on that before we get married."

input:
Make the Protector Visible

It's two in the morning, your little one is lonely, and the ex who dumped you by text is one text away. The Protector is the one who puts the phone in the other room, and in the morning, "I'm glad you're here" is a lot easier for your little one to believe.

Most of the Protector's job is that ordinary, and your little one can see it. You set one boundary, or say no to something costly. You deal with the bank letters you've been leaving face down, keep one small promise, clean your room. None of it feels like much. But acts like these add up to trust, and soothing with no follow-through sounds to your little one like the same unreliability that hurt them in the first place. Leaving a relationship that keeps wearing down your safety belongs on the list too, though it's much bigger than the rest.

The job has an inside half too. A surge of fear, rage, craving or shame doesn't get to decide what you say, send, spend or take, or who you sleep with or commit to. Often that means waiting while the surge tells you there isn't time. Some of the protecting happens between you and your little one, where nobody else would see it. When they get sarcastic, you don't snap back. They don't trust you, and you let them, without pushing them to reassure you.

Sometimes they complain that you only come around when something's wrong, and they're right, and you tell them so. After you've called yourself an idiot in an empty kitchen, you go back and apologize to them. Your little one sees these as clearly as a tidy room or a kept appointment. Not retaliating is evidence that you love them, though it doesn't replace loving them. If the Nurturer hasn't shown up yet, the Protector can start the relationship on its own. At first, care might be a locked door, a meal, a cancelled obligation, and it can be a while before any of it feels warm.

Pick one act and decide when you'll do it, how small the first step can be, and what help it needs, whether that's a friend sitting next to you while you open the bank letters or an hour when nobody needs anything from you. Make the Protector Visible

Protecting your little ones are you setting boundaries? Dealing with those letters from the bank, keeping a promise, cleaning your room – these things demonstrate your trustworthiness to your little one.
